idiom_name: abstract layer base type: shared state, provided behavior, required operations
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define one abstract type that names what every member of the layer shares - identity, versioning, audit fields, lifecycle hooks, equality rules - and declare on it both the members the layer provides (concrete implementations) and the members each layer member must supply (abstract operations). Derive every type in the layer from it so clients, mappers, controllers and test scaffolding can work against the supertype alone. Keep the base abstract so it can never be instantiated, keep its state private behind protected hooks instead of open fields, and document which operations subclasses may override. Where the language cannot express a common base - or the single superclass slot must stay free - substitute the nearest mechanism that still declares one type for the layer: a trait or mixin with default methods, an interface plus shared helper, or an embedded base value. Admit a member only when the whole layer needs it; the base is the layer's contract, not its utility drawer.
code_sketch:
layer_object:
    id                     # shared state, established at creation
    version
    touch()                # provided behavior: identical for every member
    describe()             # required behavior: each member implements it

member "user" extends layer_object:
    describe() -> "user <id>"

# clients, mappers and frameworks depend on layer_object alone
pitfalls: Letting the base become the layer's helper dumping ground instead of its declared contract.
Calling overridable members from the creation path, so subclasses run before they are initialised.
Absorbing another layer's concerns (persistence in a domain base, transport in a service base).
Exposing JPA @Entity or Django model specifics in the base: if the base carries @GeneratedValue(strategy=IDENTITY) or abstract=True, it cannot be reused outside that framework layer.

Returning mutable collections from getter fields (List, Set, Map): any caller who holds the reference can modify the object's state; always return defensive copies or immutable wrappers from the base.

Adding business logic to the base that requires knowledge of the subclass's specific fields: the base should manage its own state and declared hooks; violating this causes circular dependencies between layer members.
Inadvertently making the base non-abstract by adding a concrete field or default implementation that a subclass inherits unchanged, masking a missing override.

Wrong move: make a framework-specific persistence base (such as a JPA mapped superclass or Django abstract model) the domain layer's universal base -> Y fails: ORM annotations, lifecycle callbacks and constructor/table assumptions leak across the boundary and make the domain hard to reuse -> instead Z: keep the mapped base in the persistence layer and expose domain ports or composition.

Wrong move: evolve a public base method or protected field without treating subclasses as clients -> Y fails: inherited self-calls and implementation changes can silently alter subclass behavior (the fragile-base-class problem) -> instead Z: seal the base or members, or document and test the small set of extension points.

Wrong move: put operations in the base that only some members can honor -> Y fails: clients typed to the supertype must downcast or receive invalid behavior, breaking substitutability -> instead Z: keep the contract minimal and split optional capabilities into interfaces or composed collaborators.
